messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Darkness: Dark spaces, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Keoni Kalani, a sixty-three-year-old financial analyst living with his wife in a suburban California home, had never expected that a single night on the highway would upend his life. The accident happened on a rain-slicked stretch of Interstate 5, just past midnight. A semi-truck drifted into his lane, and Keoni’s sedan was forced into the guardrail, spinning before it came to rest in the darkness of an unlit embankment. He remembered the smell of gasoline mixing with the metallic tang of his own blood, the screech of twisting metal still ringing in his ears long after the sound had stopped. He had been trapped in the driver’s seat for nearly forty minutes, the interior of his car dark except for the faint glow of the hazard lights, his mind racing, his body trembling. When the paramedics finally cut him free, he could not stop replaying the moment of impact—the way his body had known something was wrong before his thoughts had caught up.

In the weeks after his physical recovery, Keoni tried to return to his normal routine. He went back to the downtown office where he spent his days analyzing market trends, but the world around him had changed. The first time a coworker microwaved leftover stir-fry, the faint scent of something smoky filled the break room, and Keoni felt his chest tighten and his palms go slick before he could even identify why. He had come to believe that his body reacted to danger before his mind had a chance to think—and that was the most frightening part. He began to notice the darkness of the parking garage at the end of his shift, the way the elevator doors closed, the sudden roar of a passing motorcycle on the street below his window. Each time, it was as though the memory of the accident was not a memory at all, but something that was happening right then, in the present. He would hear the screech of metal, the hiss of the airbag, the sound of his own ragged breathing, and for a moment he was back inside that crumpled car.

Keoni stopped driving. He told his wife that traffic made him anxious, but the real reason went deeper: he was certain that if he let his mind drift while behind the wheel, he would lose control entirely. He started taking the train, but even there he could not relax. As soon as he entered any room—the office conference room, a restaurant, a waiting area—his eyes would go automatically to the exits, counting the doors, measuring the distance to the stairwell. He found himself waking in the middle of the night, not from a nightmare but from a sudden, alert certainty that something was wrong, and he would sit up in the dark, listening, feeling the need to check that the bedroom door was still closed, that the house was still safe.

Keoni avoided thinking about the accident. He had told himself that if he let the memory in, he would not be able to handle it—that it would consume him, that he would unravel completely. So he kept himself busy, focused on spreadsheets and quarterly reports, walked quickly through the office halls, and never talked about what had happened. But the avoidance came at a cost. His wife, with whom he had always shared a quiet, comfortable life, began to notice that he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind, that he no longer wanted to go out for dinner, that he insisted on leaving every light in the house on at night. She tried to ask him about it, but he shut down, offering only vague reassurances. At work, a colleague commented that Keoni seemed “on edge all the time,” and a junior analyst remarked that he was always looking over his shoulder like he expected an attack.

It was a vendor’s coffee cart outside the office that finally broke through. One morning, a sweet, oily smell—something like burnt coffee and gasoline—drifted up from the street. Keoni was reaching for the lobby door when the scent hit him, and suddenly he was back in the car: the darkness, the ringing silence after the wreck, the smell of fuel soaking his clothes. He stood frozen, his heart pounding, unable to move, and it was several seconds before he realized that a colleague was calling his name. That afternoon, he made an appointment with a therapist. He did not know if talking about the accident would help or hurt, but he knew he could not keep living this way—always on guard, always scanning, always afraid that the next smell, the next sound, the next dark room would pull him back into a night he could not escape.
